Renato, good afternoon. I am closing the delegate list for Boston tomorrow. Are you coming?
Good afternoon, Priya. Yes, I am writing to confirm my attendance on both days.
Perfect. The itinerary was sent with the invitation, but people never open it, so let me say the two important parts.
Please do. I read the dates and the venue, and I stopped there.

Everybody does. First: badges are collected on site, at the desk, from seven thirty. Second: a shuttle is provided from the hotel every thirty minutes. And day two is not the keynote, it is breakouts.
That is the part I wanted to ask about. Which breakout am I expected to take part in? I would be happy to present the results from the South and Southeast of Brazil.
You are in the Latin America group, on the second morning. And thank you for offering. Most managers reply with one word, and then they are surprised when nobody knows who they are.
Is one slide still the rule? And is it hosted by the global team, or by the region?
One slide, and it is hosted by the global team. Send it to me by the first of March and I will have it printed for the room.

I have been going to these global meetings for about twelve years, and the first thing I tell people is that the agenda is not the meeting. The sessions are useful, and the keynote is usually good, but the conversations that change something happen in the twenty minutes between them. That is when you meet the person who signs off on your budget, or the colleague in another country who has already solved the problem you are stuck on. So my advice is simple. Read the delegate list before you fly. Choose three people you want to speak to, and find out one real thing about their market. Then, when you are on site, do not have lunch with your own country team every day. You already know them. Sit somewhere else. And one last thing, about English. Nobody at these meetings speaks perfect English, and nobody cares. What people remember is whether you had something to say about your own market. Prepare two sentences about yours and you will be fine.

I organise four of these meetings a year, and delegates forget the same three things every time. The first is the confirmation. The invitation asks you to confirm attendance by a date, and that date is not decoration. Rooms are booked from that number, and the airport transfers are arranged from that number too. If you confirm late you will still come, but you may be put in a hotel twenty minutes away from everybody else. The second is the badge. It is collected on site, at the desk, on the first morning, and it is needed for every room in the building. People arrive at nine, walk straight to the first session, and are stopped at the door. And the third is the breakout. Delegates read the keynote and the plenary sessions carefully, and then they ignore the breakouts, which is exactly where they are expected to speak. If your name is printed next to a breakout, you are not the audience. You are part of it.

Thank you for the invitation to the Global Commercial Meeting in Boston. I am writing to confirm my attendance on both days. Could you confirm which breakout I am expected to take part in? I would be happy to present the results from the South and Southeast of Brazil.
